newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel votes new U.S. ag research plan.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel votes new U.S. ag research plan.

text.p: Federal spending on agricultural research should rise by nearly 20 percent to assist high-profile projects like gene mapping and biotech foods, the Senate Agriculture Committee decided Wednesday.
Senators approved the increase of $980 million over five years as part of a comprehensive bill to reauthorize federal ag research programs. The bill now goes to the Senate floor for a vote.

The lion's share of new spending -- $780 million -- would be devoted to an Initiative for Future Agriculture and Food Systems to tackle food safety, mapping of genes in food crops and livestock, biotech foods, "precision" farming and conservation. It would be guaranteed funding, not subject to an appropriations vote each yar.

"This bill really has to be the catalyst for a worldwide upgrading and expansion of agricultural research," chairman Richard Lugar (R-Ind.) said, citing projections that yields must triple in 50 years to feed the burgeoning world population.

Larger spending on ag research would be offset by cuts in funding to administer the food stamp program, an $82 million reduction in Agriculture Department computer purchases and savings by allowing some haying and grazing on Conservation Reserve land.
Agricultural research is widely regarded as the foundation of the efficient and profilic U.S. farm sector.

Iowa Senator Tom Harkin, Democratic leader on the committee, said the research bill "will be the most important bill...in several years" for the committee, even outranking the 1990 and 1996 laws that set overall U.S. farm policy.

The federal government spends about $1 billion a year on its own ag research and in grants to universities and scientists. There have been questions in recent years if the money was spent to best effect.

To encourage more effective use of research money, the committee-approved bill would require in most cases that one-fourth of research and extension funds be spent on multistate projects. The Agriculture Department would be directed to gather ideas from the farm, food and research sectors for setting research priorities.
In general, research projects would have to have national or regional application to qualify for funding.
A House Agriculture subcommittee has held several hearings on ag research but has yet to draft a reauthorization bill.
